nameStory: This tiny algae doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists simply call it by its scientific name, Coenochloris fottii. The genus name Coenochloris comes from Greek words meaning 'shared green,' referring to how these microscopic organisms live together in colonies. It was named after Dr. Fott, a researcher who studied freshwater algae.
description: Coenochloris fottii is a microscopic freshwater algae that you'll never see with the naked eye - it's far too small! These tiny green organisms live in colonies, forming slimy films or greenish tints in still water. Each individual cell is roughly spherical and contains bright green chloroplasts that help it photosynthesize like plants do. You'd need a microscope to actually observe the details of this species.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual cells are only visible under magnification - you'll only notice their presence as a greenish tint or film in water

idTips.label: Colonial growth
idTips.description: Forms loose colonies that create a slimy, slippery feeling when touched and may produce a faint earthy smell

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Creates a distinct emerald-green coloration in water, more vibrant than typical pond scum

idTips.label: Still water preference
idTips.description: Found in calm, non-flowing water bodies where it can form undisturbed films on the surface

habitat: This microscopic algae lives in freshwater environments like small ponds, temporary pools, and quiet backwaters of streams throughout New England. It prefers nutrient-rich water in partially shaded areas where organic matter has accumulated. Look for it in woodland pools, farm ponds, and marshy areas where water moves slowly or sits still.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures rise and daylight increases, creating faint greenish tints in warming pools.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when colonies are most visible as green films on water surfaces, especially during warm, still periods.
seasonality.fall: Populations decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases, though some colonies may persist in protected areas.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive or dormant, surviving as resistant cells that will restart growth when conditions improve.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single drop of pond water can contain thousands of these tiny organisms - meaning you've probably walked past millions of them without ever knowing they were there!
confusionNotes: Since this species requires microscopic identification, it's easily confused with other microscopic green algae that create similar greenish films in water. The specific cellular structure and arrangement can only be distinguished under proper magnification by trained observers.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents the often-overlooked microscopic world that forms the foundation of freshwater ecosystems. While we tend to focus on plants and animals we can see, these tiny algae are actually the primary producers that support entire food webs in New England's ponds and streams.
compareHints: Since there are no other Coenochloris species documented in New England, this algae is best compared to other colonial green algae like Scenedesmus or Pediastrum. Unlike those species which form distinct geometric colonies, Coenochloris fottii creates looser, more irregular groupings of cells. The specific cellular arrangement and shape can only be reliably distinguished under microscopic examination.
